title: The Cave, the Silence, and the Book That Says He Wrote It
years: fl. 2nd century CE (birth and death years unattested)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Roman Palestine, a birth no source records
stops.date_confidence: No date. No tannaitic, amoraic, or contemporary source gives his birth year or his birthplace; the ISO date here is an ordering placeholder with no evidentiary value whatever. Popular reference works print c. 90 CE, which is a modern back-calculation from the discipleship and death traditions rather than a source-based date, and it is not used anywhere in this file.
stops.campa: A boy is born somewhere in Roman Palestine to a man named Yochai, and the whole record of the birth is the patronymic. No town claims him. No year is written down. No inscription cut anywhere in the province carries his name. Everything that will be known of him arrives later, in other men's mouths, in academies not yet founded, in recensions redacted centuries after he is dead. The earliest thing anyone can say about him with a source behind it is that his father was called Yochai.
sources: Absence of primary attestation; scholarly consensus per Lee I. Levine and Ben-Zion Rosenfeld
suggested_refs: The standard reference works' 'c. 90 CE', traceable to back-calculation rather than to any source

stops.name: Bnei Brak, the house of Rabbi Akiva
stops.date_confidence: Inference, and declared as one. Akiva's best-attested base is Bnei Brak (Sanhedrin 32b), but no source says Rashbi studied there; the pin follows Akiva's known location rather than any statement about the pupil. The year is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Rabbi Akiva keeps a house of study on the coastal plain, and the students who will carry the Mishnah into the next generation pass through it. Shimon bar Yochai is counted among them, though no sugya sets him at this particular door on any named day. What he takes from the place is a method before it is a doctrine: that every particle of the text is deliberate, that nothing in it is filler, that a crown on a letter can be argued from. He will use that method for the rest of his life, on Akiva's own readings among others.
sources: Mishnah and Tosefta passim (discipleship transmitted, not autograph)
suggested_refs: Bnei Brak as Akiva's attested base, against Yevamot 62b's placement of the five in the South

stops.name: Palestine, the star that goes forth from Jacob
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Rashbi transmits the tradition (Yerushalmi Ta'anit 4:5). Not attested, and expressly not inferred here, that he fought in, endorsed, or witnessed the revolt. The date is the securely established start of the war per Cassius Dio and the archaeology at Battir, not a date for the transmission.
stops.campa: Akiva looks at Bar Koziba and reads Numbers over him: a star shall go forth from Jacob. The oracle names a king. The line that carries Akiva's reading down to us runs through Shimon bar Yochai, who transmits it, and transmitting it is the whole of what the record says he did with it. No source puts him in the field. The war runs three years and ends with Hadrian's legions at Beitar, the province renamed Syria Palaestina, and Jews forbidden their own city.
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 69.12-14, via adriano.journey.json
suggested_refs: Beitar (Khirbet el-Yahud), 31.7247 / 35.1339, the war's end on Hadrian's own file
Jerusalem, 31.778 / 35.2354, the city barred after 135/136

stops.name: The prison of Akiva, Rabbi, teach me Torah
stops.date_confidence: The exchange is attested (Bavli Pesachim 112a); the place is not. The text names no city at all. Caesarea, the Roman provincial capital, is where later tradition puts Akiva's imprisonment and execution, and the pin follows that tradition while the sugya itself stays silent. The year sits inside the war years for ordering only.
stops.campa: Rome has forbidden the teaching of Torah and Akiva is in a cell for having taught it. His student comes and asks to be taught. Akiva refuses, saying the danger is real. Shimon answers with a threat: that he will tell his father Yochai, who has the ear of the government, and have the old man handed over. It is the only glimpse the corpus ever gives of Yochai, a father with access to the authorities, and it is a Babylonian storyteller's touch rather than a fact about any household.
stops.quote_source: Bavli Pesachim 112a, R. Shimon bar Yochai to the imprisoned R. Akiva, Sefaria translation
suggested_refs: The Caesarea tradition of Akiva's imprisonment, wholly extra-textual to Pesachim 112a

stops.name: The prison of Akiva, the calf and the cow
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Bavli Pesachim 112a). The location is again unstated in the source and the pin follows the later Caesarea tradition. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The teacher answers the threat with an image out of a barn. More than the calf wishes to suck, the cow wants to suckle; the wanting runs the other way too, and harder. Shimon presses him: the risk is not yours, you are already in prison, it is mine to take. Akiva teaches him. What he teaches, in the Bavli's account, is not mysticism. It is two practical maxims. If you wish to strangle yourself, hang yourself on a tall tree. And when you teach your son, teach him from a corrected text.
stops.quote: More than the calf wishes to suck, the cow wants to suckle, but I am afraid of the danger.
stops.quote_source: Bavli Pesachim 112a, R. Akiva to R. Shimon bar Yochai, Sefaria translation
suggested_refs: The maxims Akiva gives once he relents, Pesachim 112a

stops.name: The South of Judea, the five who were left
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the tradition (Bavli Yevamot 62b), not for the pin: the sugya names only 'the South', darom, with no site, and the coordinate is a regional approximation for southern Judea. In the sugya the earlier deaths run from Passover to Shavuot and Rav Nahman attributes them to diphtheria, not to the revolt; later tradition conflates the two and this file does not.
stops.campa: Twelve thousand pairs of Akiva's students die in a single season, from Passover to Shavuot, because they did not treat each other with respect. Torah is desolate. The old man goes south to the sages there and teaches five: Meir, Yehuda ben Ilai, Yose ben Halafta, Shimon bar Yochai, Elazar ben Shammua. Of these five the Talmud says that they upheld the study of Torah at that time. It does not say where in the south they were sitting, and it does not name the town.
suggested_refs: The sugya's darom, unlocated, against the popular placement of the scene at Bnei Brak

stops.name: A Palestinian academy, four readings against his teacher
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction from tannaitic material (Tosefta Sotah 6:6; Sifre Devarim 31:8). No place and no date are given by either source; the pin stands for an unspecified Palestinian academy setting and the year orders the segment.
stops.campa: In four places he takes an interpretation of Akiva's, sets his own beside it, and argues that his own is the better reading. He does this while calling the man his teacher, and while transmitting his teacher's traditions faithfully elsewhere. Tosefta Sotah and Sifre Devarim set the two gestures down side by side and pass no comment on either. Whether the tannaim who transmitted them saw any tension there is not a thing the texts let anyone find out.
suggested_refs: The four disputed interpretations, read as evidence of independence within discipleship

stops.name: Palestine, marketplaces and bridges and bathhouses
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Bavli Shabbat 33b). The sugya gives no place, no date, and crucially no emperor: it says only Caesar. Identifying him with Hadrian is a later inference and is not made here. The year orders the segment.
stops.campa: Three sages sit talking about what Rome has built. Yehuda calls the works fine: marketplaces, bridges, bathhouses. Yose says nothing at all. Shimon says Rome built every one of them for itself, marketplaces to put prostitutes in, bathhouses to groom its own bodies, bridges to take a toll at. Yehuda, son of converts, is listening, and he repeats it. The government answers each man according to his sentence. Yehuda is made head of the speakers everywhere, Yose is exiled to Tzippori, and Shimon is condemned to death.
suggested_refs: The sugya's unnamed Caesar, routinely and wrongly filled in as Hadrian

stops.name: The study hall, bread and water from a wife
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Bavli Shabbat 33b). The sugya gives no location for the study hall. His wife is never named anywhere in the corpus, and this episode is the whole of her record.
stops.campa: Father and son hide first in the beit midrash, not in any wilderness. A woman carries them a loaf and a jug of water each day and walks home again. She is his wife. The corpus that will supply him with four separate personae, wonder-worker and magician and scholar and saint, preserves of her exactly this: bread, water, the walk there, the walk back. It does not give her a name. When the decree tightens he judges that the women are soft-hearted and may be broken into telling, and they go.
suggested_refs: Ben-Zion Rosenfeld on the four cumulative personae of Rashbi in the sources

stops.name: Peki'in, they went and hid in a cave
stops.date_confidence: Attested that they flee to a cave (Bavli Shabbat 33b; Yerushalmi Sheviit 9:1; Genesis Rabbah 79:6). No talmudic source names the cave or locates it; the identification with Peki'in in the Upper Galilee is later folk tradition, and the pin follows that tradition while saying so.
stops.campa: They go into the rock. From this point the record splits in two and never rejoins: one telling out of the land itself, one out of the academies of Babylonia, differing on how long they stay, what feeds them, how they learn it is safe, and what they are when they come out. Both agree on the cave and on the son. Neither names the hill. Centuries afterwards a village in the Upper Galilee will claim the site, without one talmudic sentence behind the claim.
stops.quote: They went and they hid in a cave. A miracle occurred and a carob tree was created for them as well as a spring of water.
suggested_refs: The Peki'in cave tradition, medieval and local, with no talmudic warrant

stops.name: The cave, carobs until the sores came
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Palestinian recension (Yerushalmi Sheviit 9:1; Genesis Rabbah 79:6), which gives thirteen continuous years with no return to the cave. The dates are ordering devices; no source dates either the flight or the emergence.
stops.campa: Thirteen years, one stretch, no reprieve in the middle. The Palestinian telling is sparing with miracles and exact about the body: they eat withered carobs until they break out in sores. There is no heavenly voice sending them back, no burning gaze, no reconciliation scene at the end of it. There is a father, a son, a rock, and a diet that damages the skin of the men living on it. What they study in those thirteen years is not described anywhere in either source.
stops.quote: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai and Rabbi Elazar his son were hiding in a cave for thirteen years during the days of persecution.
suggested_refs: Jeffrey L. Rubenstein and Ofra Meir on the Palestinian-to-Babylonian development of the cave cycle

stops.name: The cave mouth, the fowler and the two words
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Palestinian recension (Yerushalmi Sheviit 9:1; Genesis Rabbah 79:6). The research pool's first pass described a providential pair of birds acting as an all-clear about officials; the sources have one fowler and a lesson in providence. The year is thirteen after the flight, an ordering device only.
stops.campa: At the end of the thirteen years he watches a man spreading nets for birds. A voice out of heaven says one of two words over each bird: dimus, acquitted, and it lifts away through the mesh; spekula, killing, and it is taken. He counts the verdicts and reasons upward from them. If no sparrow is caught without a sentence pronounced over it, then no man is either. He leaves the cave on that reasoning. In this telling nobody comes up the hill to tell him anything.
stops.quote: He saw a certain hunter standing and hunting birds. When Rabbi Shimon would hear a Divine Voice from Heaven: 'Freedom, freedom,' it would escape.
suggested_refs: Charlotte Fonrobert's reading of the cave against Plato's allegory
Michal Bar-Asher Siegal on ascetic retreat in late-antique Christian monastic literature

stops.name: Tiberias, the lupines on the water
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Palestinian recension (Yerushalmi Sheviit 9:1; Genesis Rabbah 79:6), where the method is lupines. The Bavli's Tiberias scene at Shabbat 34a uses hard and soft ground instead and does not employ lupines here at all. Lee I. Levine treats this episode as the one plausible historical kernel in the whole cycle; that is a scholarly proposal, not a finding.
stops.campa: The city on the lake is built over graves nobody mapped, so no priest can live in it without contracting corpse impurity. His son puts it as a debt: the town fed us, and we are leaving it unclean. Lee I. Levine treats this as the one episode in the whole cycle a modern historian can argue actually happened, a man with a plant and a survey rather than a miracle. Shimon cuts up lupines and scatters them on standing water, and where a body lies underneath the pieces float, and he marks the ground.
stops.quote: Tiberias has afforded us so much benefit, and we are not purifying it from the dead?
stops.quote_source: Genesis Rabbah 79:6, R. Eleazar b. R. Shimon to his father, Sefaria translation
sources: Lee I. Levine on Roman Tiberias
suggested_refs: Genesis Rabbah 79:6's opening maxim on gratitude to a place from which one benefits, echoed at Tiberias

stops.name: Magdala, the Samaritan and the scribe made bones
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Palestinian recension (Yerushalmi Sheviit 9:1; Genesis Rabbah 79:6), which the research pool's first pass had misassigned to Bavli Shabbat 34a. The Bavli has an anonymous elder and Yehuda ben Gerim in these roles instead. The two recensions are left unharmonized.
stops.campa: A Samaritan takes a corpse and buries it in ground Shimon has just pronounced clean, then produces it, to show the old Jew up. At Magdala a scribe mocks the purification out loud in front of people. This is the same man who reasoned from a caught sparrow that judgment is everywhere and exact. The Yerushalmi and Genesis Rabbah record what he does about the mockery without a word of comment or apology. He looks at the scribe, and the scribe becomes a heap of bones in the road.
suggested_refs: Bavli Shabbat 34a, where the mocker is an anonymous elder and the bones are Yehuda ben Gerim's

segments.name: Twelve Years and Twelve Months: the Babylonian Telling

stops.name: The cave, buried to the neck in sand
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Babylonian recension (Bavli Shabbat 33b), which gives twelve years plus a further twelve months, and a spring alongside the carob tree. Its duration and details differ materially from the Palestinian version; the two are not merged here. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The Bavli furnishes the cave. A carob tree springs up and a spring of water opens. It also solves a problem the Palestinian telling never raises: they have one set of clothes each and no way to replace them, so they strip, bury themselves to the neck in sand, and study like that through the day, dressing only to pray. The count here is twelve years, not the thirteen the Palestinian sources give, and the sand belongs to this recension alone. Two heads above it, the text going back and forth between them in the dark.
stops.quote: They would remove their clothes and sit covered in sand up to their necks. They would study Torah all day in that manner.
suggested_refs: The sand detail, unique to the Babylonian recension

stops.name: The mouth of the cave, Elijah with the news
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Babylonian recension only (Bavli Shabbat 33b). The Palestinian version has no Elijah and no announcement; there the departure is reasoned out from the fowler. The year is set twelve after the flight as an ordering device.
stops.campa: Elijah comes and stands where the cave opens and says it to the air, so that they will hear it: the emperor is dead and his decree is void. Nobody has to travel. No messenger is paid. Nothing is checked against anything. The Bavli does not name that emperor, not here and not at the sentencing, and no later reader is entitled to name him on its behalf. The prophet who never died brings word that the man who sentenced Shimon to death has died himself, and the two of them come up out of the hole.
suggested_refs: The unnamed Caesar of Shabbat 33b, whose death is reported but whose identity the sugya withholds

stops.name: Outside the cave, whatever they looked at burned
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Babylonian recension only (Bavli Shabbat 33b-34a). There is no parallel in the Palestinian telling, which has neither the burning gaze nor the return to the cave.
stops.campa: They come out into a country of men plowing and sowing, and are appalled: eternal life set down, temporal life picked up. Wherever the two of them look, the place burns. Twelve years of nothing but text has made them lethal to ordinary work. The voice that answers is not on their side: it asks whether they left the cave in order to wreck the world, and sends them back into it for twelve months. The men in the fields are not addressed at all, and go on plowing and sowing.
stops.quote: A Divine Voice emerged and said to them: Did you emerge from the cave in order to destroy My world? Return to your cave.
suggested_refs: Jeffrey L. Rubenstein, Talmudic Stories, on the Bavli's reworking of the emergence

stops.name: A field at Sabbath eve, two bundles of myrtle
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Babylonian recension only (Bavli Shabbat 33b-34a). The old man, the myrtles, and the reconciliation they produce have no counterpart in the Palestinian telling.
stops.campa: The second emergence is calmer. Eleazar's look still burns, and his father heals behind him whatever the son destroys. Then at dusk on a Friday an old man goes past at a run holding two branches of myrtle. Why two? One for Remember and one for Observe, the two verbs in which the commandment about the Sabbath is given. Shimon turns to his son and says: see how precious the commandments are to Israel. The burning ends there, in a field, over a man carrying twigs home.
stops.quote: one corresponding to 'Remember' and one corresponding to 'Observe'
suggested_refs: Exodus 20:8 and Deuteronomy 5:12, the two verbs the myrtles answer to

stops.name: Tiberias, hard ground, soft ground, a heap of bones
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Babylonian recension (Bavli Shabbat 34a), which differs from the Palestinian version at every point: no lupines, an anonymous elder rather than a Samaritan and a scribe of Magdala, and Yehuda ben Gerim as the one turned into bones. The contradiction is left standing.
stops.campa: The Bavli sends him to Tiberias as well, and gives him a different method: he pronounces hard ground clean and puts a marker wherever the ground is soft. An old man jeers that ben Yochai has purified a cemetery, and dies of being looked at. Then Shimon meets Yehuda ben Gerim in the street, the man whose report to the government cost him twelve years in a cave and a death sentence he never served, and fixes his eyes on him, and makes him a pile of bones on the road.
suggested_refs: Yerushalmi Sheviit 9:1, where the lupines and the Samaritan belong instead

stops.name: The Upper Galilee, Tekoa and the walk to the spring
stops.date_confidence: Attested across three tractates (Bavli Shabbat 147b; Eruvin 91a; Menachot 72a), unusually solid for this subject. The site is not: Graetz argued that Rashbi's Tekoa was Galilean and not the biblical Judean town, and nobody has located it. The pin is a regional approximation in the Upper Galilee, deliberately not a site. The studying happened in Rashbi's lifetime; only Judah ha-Nasi's recollection of it is later.
stops.campa: A circle gathers around him in a town called Tekoa, and one of the boys in it grows up to redact the Mishnah. Judah ha-Nasi remembers the place from the inside, and what he remembers is not a teaching. It is a route: oil and towels carried courtyard to roof, roof to enclosure, enclosure to spring, the whole path plotted so that nothing is carried through public ground on the Sabbath. Three separate tractates keep that memory, which makes the walk to the bath the best-attested thing in his later life. Where the town of Tekoa stood, nobody has established.
stops.quote: When we would study Torah with Rabbi Shimon in Tekoa, we would carry oil and towels from the courtyard to the roof and from the roof into an enclosure similar to a courtyard until we reached the spring in which we would bathe, without passing through a public domain.
stops.quote_source: Bavli Shabbat 147b, Judah ha-Nasi recalling his youth, Sefaria translation
suggested_refs: Graetz on the Galilean Tekoa, distinct from the Judean town of Amos

stops.name: Palestine, his son and colleague Eleazar
stops.date_confidence: Attested across both recensions and throughout the halakhic sugyot (Bavli Shabbat 33b-34a; Yerushalmi Sheviit 9:1; Genesis Rabbah 79:6). This is the one family relationship the record does not contradict itself about. The year is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Rabbi Eleazar son of Rabbi Shimon is in the cave in every version, hungry in every version, and afterwards a named authority in his own right across the halakhic material. He is the only relative the corpus is consistent about. The wife has no name in any source. The daughter appears only as somebody else's marriage, and the two traditions cannot agree whose. Yochai is a patronymic and one reported threat. Eleazar is the exception, and the sugyot cite him by name.
suggested_refs: R. Eleazar b. R. Shimon's own independent halakhic material

stops.name: Palestine, Pinhas ben Yair and a generation in dispute
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction, flagged and not resolved. Bavli Shabbat 33b states outright that Pinhas ben Yair is his son-in-law, using the word chatneih; a later Zoharic tradition makes Pinhas his father-in-law instead. The two place Pinhas in opposite generations and neither is in a position to correct the other.
stops.campa: When Shimon comes out of the cave, Pinhas ben Yair hears of it and goes out along the road to meet him. The Bavli says plainly what Pinhas is to him: chatneih, his son-in-law, married to a daughter the text never troubles to name. Centuries later the Zoharic tradition turns the relation the other way round and makes Pinhas the father-in-law, the older man, the one who gives a daughter rather than takes one. Which of them married into the other's house, and which way the generations run between them, is a question both traditions answer and neither is in a position to settle.
suggested_refs: The chatneih of Shabbat 33b against the Zohar's father-in-law

stops.name: Palestine, Torah as the whole of the day
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Bavli Berakhot 35b). Abaye's verdict is later amoraic, roughly fourth century, appended in the Babylonian redaction; it is a judgment on the position rather than a report from Rashbi's lifetime.
stops.campa: Rabbi Ishmael reads the verse to mean gather in your grain, and concludes that a man should combine Torah with a worldly trade. Shimon bar Yochai answers that when Israel does the will of God others do their work for them, and a man's occupation should be the text and nothing besides. It is the most radical position in the tractate, and thirteen years in a cave with a carob tree is what it looks like carried out. Generations later Abaye takes a count of who lived by which opinion and how each group fared at their studies.
stops.quote: Although there is room for both opinions, many have acted in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael, and combined working for a living and learning Torah, and although they engaged in activities other than the study of Torah, were successful in their Torah study. Many have acted in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai and were not successful in their Torah study.
suggested_refs: The derekh eretz position of R. Yishmael, against which the ruling is set

stops.name: Palestine, from the day I was created
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a saying transmitted in his name (Bavli Sukkah 45b), which is not the same thing as a record of him saying it. The claim in the sugya is graduated in three steps; the research pool's first pass flattened it and added a reference to Sinai that appears nowhere in the passage, and that phrase is dropped.
stops.campa: The claim comes in three sizes. Alone, he can absolve the world of everything since the day he himself was made. With his son beside him, since the day the world was made. With Yotam ben Uzziah added to the pair, from the world's beginning to its end. Elsewhere he says he has seen the members of the caste of the spiritually prominent and they are few: if they number a thousand, he and his son are among them; if they number a hundred, the same; and if they number two, they are the two.
stops.quote: I am able to absolve the entire world from judgment for sins committed from the day I was created until now.
stops.quote_source: Bavli Sukkah 45b, in the name of R. Shimon b. Yohai, Sefaria translation
suggested_refs: The bnei aliyah saying at Sukkah 45b, a separate tradition from the absolution

stops.name: Rome, a man accustomed to miracles
stops.date_confidence: The text is attested (Bavli Meilah 17b); the historicity is not. No Roman source records any such embassy or any such decree, and the episode is hagiographic in character, the latest layer of the Babylonian redaction. The date is an ordering device with no evidentiary basis at all.
stops.campa: A decree comes down against the Jews and somebody has to go to the capital and get it lifted. The sages choose him, and the reason they give is not that he is learned or well spoken. It is that miracles happen to him. He sails with Eleazar ben Yose. On the way a demon called Ben Temalion catches them up and proposes an arrangement: he will enter the emperor's daughter, Shimon will drive him out, and the favor will be theirs to name. Shimon takes the offer, even through a demon.
stops.quote: Let Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai go to Rome, as he is accustomed to experiencing miracles.
suggested_refs: The absence of any Roman documentary trace of the embassy or the decree

stops.name: The palace at Rome, ben Temalion emerge
stops.date_confidence: Attested as text (Bavli Meilah 17b); not as history. The research pool's first pass gave two calls and a granting of favor in the abstract; the sugya has three calls and the physical destruction of the letter of decrees in the imperial treasury.
stops.campa: The emperor's daughter is possessed and nobody in Rome can help her. Shimon is brought in and calls the demon by name three times, and it comes out of her, and she is well. No Roman archive corroborates a word of this, nor the embassy, nor the decree it is meant to have annulled. The emperor takes the two of them down into his treasury and tells them to take whatever they want. They walk past everything else in the room, find the letter that carries the decrees against the Jews, and tear the letter up.
stops.quote: Ben Temalyon, emerge! Ben Temalyon, emerge!
stops.quote_source: Bavli Meilah 17b, R. Shimon bar Yochai's exorcism formula, Sefaria translation
suggested_refs: Ben-Zion Rosenfeld on the wonder-worker and magician registers layered onto the scholar

segments.name: The Texts That Carry His Name

stops.name: Palestine, the anonymous Sifre is declared his
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a redactional rule stated by the Bavli (Sanhedrin 86a). It is a school attribution made retrospectively by later editors, not a claim that Rashbi composed the Sifre, and the two must never be conflated.
stops.campa: Later editors, sorting a mass of unattributed halakhic midrash, lay down a rule: an anonymous passage in the Sifre follows Rabbi Shimon. It is a filing decision, made centuries after him, about how to read silence. Its effect is to assign him a book. A saying quoted in his name is one thing and a text filed under his school is a different thing, and the gap between them will only widen once men begin putting revelations in his mouth. Sanhedrin 86a is where the filing starts.
suggested_refs: The stam Sifre rule as a redactional convention rather than an authorship claim

stops.name: The school of Rabbi Shimon, a book reassembled from quotations
stops.date_confidence: The underlying tradition is tannaitic; the surviving text is not. The Mekhilta de-Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai has no continuous medieval manuscript. It was reconstructed by David Zvi Hoffmann in 1905, then by J. N. Epstein and E. Z. Melamed, and translated critically by W. David Nelson (JPS, 2006), out of citations in Midrash ha-Gadol and geniza fragments. The stop's date orders the segment; the reconstruction is modern.
stops.campa: A halakhic midrash on Exodus carries his name and transmits the Akivan way of reading. It does not survive. No medieval scribe hands it on whole; it drops out of circulation and exists only as sentences quoted inside other people's compilations and as torn leaves in a Cairo storeroom. Scholars put it back together out of those pieces, one quotation at a time, and print it. What stands on the shelf under his name is a modern object assembled from debris.
sources: D. Z. Hoffmann, Mechilta de-Rabbi Simon b. Jochai (1905)
J. N. Epstein and E. Z. Melamed, critical edition
W. D. Nelson, Mekhilta de-Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai (JPS, 2006)
suggested_refs: Midrash ha-Gadol and the Cairo Geniza fragments, the sources of the reconstruction

stops.name: Unknown, a death with no narrative
stops.date_confidence: No date, no place, no cause. No talmudic source narrates his death at all, and the ISO date here is an ordering placeholder with no evidentiary value. The only death-scene anywhere in the tradition is the Idra Zuta's, a Castilian composition of roughly eleven hundred years later.
stops.campa: He dies. Nothing else about it is recorded anywhere: not the year, not the town, not the illness, not the age, not who was in the room. The corpus that will supply him with a demon in Rome, a spring in a cave, and a gaze that reduces men to bone has no sentence at all for the end of his own life. Neither Talmud narrates the death, and no midrash marks the day. The silence stays open for eleven hundred years. What fills it then is written in Castile, in Aramaic, by somebody else.
sources: Absence of any tannaitic, amoraic, or early death-narrative
suggested_refs: Zohar, Idra Zuta, the mystical death-scene composed in Castile

stops.name: Peki'in, a vision put in his mouth under a new empire
stops.date_confidence: Explicit pseudepigraphy, and the direction of reference runs forward from his life. The Nistarot de-Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai is placed by scholarship in the seventh or eighth century on internal evidence of early Islamic politics, not on a colophon; 750 is a midpoint of that range and not an attested date. The stop sits at the cave because the text sets itself there. Rashbi was some six centuries dead.
stops.campa: Arab armies take the province, and an apocalypse appears written in the first person of a man dead six hundred years. It puts him back in the cave and has him shown what is coming: kingdoms rising and falling, the last of them recognizably the one whose horsemen are outside the door while the author writes. The device works because he is already the man the tradition put underground for thirteen years, and a hiding place is where revelations get received. Whoever wrote it did not sign it, and no one has recovered the name since.
sources: Nistarot de-Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai; standard dating in the scholarship on Hebrew apocalyptic
suggested_refs: The early Islamic political references that date the text against its own claim

stops.name: Meron, a grave the Talmud never mentions
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and forward of his life. No tannaitic or talmudic source attests a tomb of Rashbi at Meron or anywhere else; the tomb tradition and its pilgrimage are medieval and early modern. The date marks the broad earliest horizon of that veneration rather than any attested event.
stops.campa: A tomb appears in the Upper Galilee with his name on it. Nothing in the Mishnah, the Tosefta, or either Talmud knows anything about it. Pilgrims come anyway, first a trickle and then in numbers, to a whitewashed building on a hillside a few kilometers from the village that claims his cave. The earliest records of the site are medieval pilgrimage itineraries, written by men who walked to it and described what they found there. Before those, on this hill, nothing.
sources: Absence of Meron burial tradition in Mishnah, Tosefta, Bavli, and Yerushalmi
Elchanan Reiner on the Meron cult
suggested_refs: The medieval and early-modern pilgrimage itineraries that first record the site

stops.name: Meron, the book that says he wrote it
stops.date_confidence: Interpretive status stated plainly, and the reference runs forward from his life. The Zoharic corpus is dated by the prevailing critical current (Scholem, refined by Liebes, Huss, Meroz) to late 13th or early 14th century Castile, on Aramaic grammatical errors, Arabic and Spanish loanwords, and unfamiliarity with the geography of the Land of Israel. The stop sits at Rashbi's own traditional pin because the writing and the circulating happened on moses_de_leon's ground, at Guadalajara 40.6333 / -3.1669 and Avila, not on his.
stops.campa: In Castile, Moses de Leon begins putting sheets into circulation, written in an Aramaic nobody has spoken for centuries and presented as an ancient book composed by Shimon bar Yochai in the cave with his son beside him. He swears the manuscript is at his house in Avila. He dies before anyone is shown it. His widow says afterwards that he wrote it out of his own head and put the old name on the title to raise the price; two of his students swear the opposite. The book becomes the foundation of Kabbalah.
sources: moses_de_leon.journey.json, the segment 'The Book Ascribed to Shimon bar Yochai'
Gershom Scholem's philological analysis; Yehuda Liebes; Boaz Huss; Ronit Meroz
Abraham Zacut, Sefer Yuhasin, reporting Isaac of Acre
suggested_refs: Isaac of Acre's inquiry, the oath at Valladolid, and the manuscript never produced

stops.name: Meron, the great assembly and the small one
stops.date_confidence: Literary construction rather than record, and forward of his life. The Idra Rabbah and Idra Zuta are sections of the Zoharic corpus composed in Castile around 1280-1300 and set dramatically at Meron in the 2nd century. Jacob Emden's Mitpachat Sefarim (Altona, 1761-68) had already challenged the attribution on internal anachronisms, from inside observant rabbinic scholarship, more than a century before academic Zohar studies began.
stops.campa: The Zohar stages two assemblies. In the great one the companions sit in a field and the secrets of the divine face are opened among them. In the small one the master is dying, and speaks until the lamp goes out. It is the death-scene the Talmud never wrote, supplied at last, in the wrong century and the wrong country, by men who signed his name to it. Jacob Emden printed a list of the anachronisms at Altona in the 1760s, from inside observant rabbinic scholarship, and was read. The attribution held.
sources: Zohar, Idra Rabbah and Idra Zuta
Boaz Huss; Yehuda Liebes; Ronit Meroz on Zohar composition
suggested_refs: Emden's list of internal anachronisms, a traditionalist critique predating academic Zohar studies

stops.name: Meron, the fires on the thirty-third day
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the 16th-century Safed shaping (Isaac Luria's circle; Hayyim Vital's writings), not for anything earlier: no source of any period ties Rashbi's death to 18 Iyyar. A textual-transmission hypothesis holds that the date may rest partly on a printing variant in Vital's Pri Etz Chadash. Elchanan Reiner has proposed, expressly as a hypothesis and not a finding, that the date and site complex migrated from older local traditions about Joshua and an earthquake. Forward of his life throughout.
stops.campa: The kabbalists of Safed fix the thirty-third day of the Omer as the day he died, and make the hillside at Meron the place to keep it. Fires are lit on the roof of the tomb, children are brought up the hill for their first haircut, wine is carried in, and within a few centuries the crowd on the night runs into the hundreds of thousands. No text older than the sixteenth century says he died on that day. No text of any age at all says he died on any day.
sources: Safed kabbalistic tradition around Isaac Luria's circle
Hayyim Vital, Pri Etz Chaim and related writings
Elchanan Reiner on the Meron hillula
suggested_refs: The printing-variant hypothesis for 18 Iyyar in Vital's Pri Etz Chadash
